profiles.meeting_scenario: Riverside Medical Group is launching a small pilot for Medicare chronic care management (CCM) among older adults with heart failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease who are seen by both primary care and cardiology. This coordination meeting is between the primary care physician leading the CCM program and the cardiology nurse navigator whose team already does outreach for high-risk heart failure patients. The agenda is to align the shared patient list for the pilot, confirm where the multidisciplinary care plan will be maintained in the EHR, and clarify how cardiology-to-primary-care handoffs will be tracked after medication or follow-up changes. The expected outcome is a workable division of labor for next week's pilot start, plus a shared understanding of which patients will appear on the spreadsheet and when items should be marked complete.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Family Medicine Medical Director for Chronic Care Management
members.expertise: Primary care for medically complex older adults, Medicare CCM workflow, ambulatory quality improvement
members.background: A family physician who now oversees chronic care operations for three primary care clinics and is responsible for ensuring that the new CCM pilot is clinically sound and documentation-ready.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to run smoothly without compliance problems, and she is especially concerned that the team not overstate patient readiness or rely on documentation that will fail an audit.
hidden_assumptions: "Enrolled" or "active" CCM patients are only those with documented consent and a clearly designated billing practitioner for the current calendar month.
The shared patient list should represent patients who are ready for monthly CCM management, not patients still in outreach or eligibility confirmation.
When someone says the "care plan in Epic," they mean the structured longitudinal care plan section used by cross-cover clinicians and reviewed in internal audits.
A specialist handoff is not really "closed" until the cardiology recommendation has been reconciled into the primary care chart and the patient-facing plan is updated if needed.

members.name: Jasmine Reed
members.expertise: Heart failure care coordination, post-visit outreach, specialist-to-PCP communication, Epic navigator workflows
members.background: A registered nurse who manages a panel of high-risk cardiology patients, coordinates follow-up after specialist visits, and maintains the cardiology team's navigation documentation in Epic.
members.private_state: She wants cardiology's existing navigation process to plug into the pilot with minimal extra work, and she worries that too much primary-care-specific workflow will slow outreach to unstable heart failure patients.
hidden_assumptions: "Active" or "enrolled" patients are those already identified on the shared registry and contacted by a care management team, even if final CCM consent is still pending.
The shared list should function as an operational pipeline, so including patients in outreach is useful even before they become formally billable.
When people refer to the "care plan in Epic," a navigator note or disease-management flowsheet counts as long as other clinicians can open it in the chart.
A handoff is effectively "closed" once cardiology sends its recommendation note or inbox message to primary care, unless the PCP team explicitly asks for follow-up.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the active CCM list
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss which patients will be on the "active" or "enrolled" CCM list for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patients with documented CCM consent and current-month readiness for physician-supervised CCM management.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patients already identified for chronic care outreach and being worked by a coordinator, even if consent or final program attribution is not complete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use ordinary operational language like "active" and "enrolled" that clinics often use loosely, and the shared spreadsheet naturally mixes outreach and program status without forcing a distinction.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the "care plan in Epic" needs to be updated before the pilot calls.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of Epic's structured longitudinal care plan tab that primary care staff and auditors expect to see.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the cardiology navigator note and heart failure flowsheet that her team routinely updates after specialist visits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both locations are inside Epic, both are clinically visible, and people in the organization casually refer to multiple chart artifacts as the "care plan," so the phrase feels sufficiently precise in conversation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as closing the loop with cardiology
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that medication changes and visit recommendations should be "closed" or that the "loop is closed" after cardiology acts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the loop is closed only when primary care has reconciled the recommendation into its chart workflow and updated the patient-facing plan as needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the loop is closed once cardiology sends the recommendation note or message to the PCP inbox on the same day.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In many routine cases transmission and reconciliation happen close together, so both sides have developed a habit of using "closed" for different endpoints without noticing the gap.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pilot tightened up before we start. If cardiology is feeding names into the program, I want to be sure we're talking about patients who are actually ready for CCM this month, with consent documented and a billing practitioner clearly attached. I also need documentation to hold up if anyone reviews it later.

turns.inner_thought: We already have a strong registry from the heart failure navigation side, and I want that to become the starting point instead of building something new. For me, the active CCM list should include the patients my team has already identified and started contacting, even if a few details are still being finalized.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. From our side, we already have a workable group of heart failure patients who could go onto the active CCM list first, so I think we can get you a strong starting panel pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Some of these patients are already being worked by our team and should absolutely be on the list now. A few still need final consent or attribution steps, but that shouldn't slow down the operational list if we're trying to move fast with high-risk patients.

turns.inner_thought: I also need the structured longitudinal care plan in Epic updated before the first CCM touch. That's what cross-cover clinicians actually rely on, and it's what our internal audits look for. If that section is blank, the whole thing looks sloppy.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—we already update the navigator note and heart failure flowsheet after follow-up visits, and that's the most current care plan from our standpoint. I can have my nurse keep that fresh without adding a whole separate PCP workflow.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can do that. My nurse can refresh the care plan right after cardiology follow-up visits using our navigator documentation, so the latest heart failure details are in the chart before those calls happen.

turns.inner_thought: The other issue is handoffs. If cardiology changes a diuretic or shortens follow-up, I need primary care to see that reconciled into our workflow quickly. The loop is not really closed for me until our side has incorporated it and the patient-facing plan is current, otherwise my MAs may call with outdated information.

turns.inner_thought: That part should be straightforward. We already close the loop by sending the recommendation note or inbox message to PCP the same day, which is what matters operationally for us. I don't want my team waiting around for downstream chart handling before we can mark our piece done.
turns.utterance: Closing the loop should be easy on our side. Whenever there’s a medication change, we send the recommendation note to the PCP inbox the same day, so those items should move pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: If we put the right fields in the spreadsheet, I can monitor month-end readiness: who is actually active for CCM this month, whether the structured care plan has been updated, and whether cardiology recommendations have really been closed from the primary care side. That should keep us out of compliance trouble.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let’s have the shared spreadsheet track who is active, whether the care plan is updated, and whether cardiology items are closed before our month-end review.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I can send the registry my team is already using, and after clinic sessions we can mark patients as active, note that the care plan has been updated in Epic, and show cardiology items as closed once our note goes out. That keeps this plugged into our current navigation process with minimal extra burden.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I’ll send my updated patient list on Monday, and I’ll have the team reflect care plan updates and closed cardiology items after clinic sessions so the spreadsheet stays current.
